notes: The scour-mistress at the Scourers' Lodge (hearthvale world life). Gives the Eighth Summer: the Chalk Hound left unscoured, the swallet, and Aldous's cord.

greet.speaker: Tamsin Hounder
greet.text: You'll have come to ask whether I'm calling them out. Everybody does. They stand at the gate and look at the cords and count them, and then they look at me. Seventy-one. You can count them yourself.

topic_1.speaker: Tamsin Hounder
topic_1.text: So it stays white. So it stays asleep. The Vale will tell you it's a festival and bring pies, and it is, and the pies are good. But my mother said the figure was cut over something that was already there, to keep it lying down, and every seventh summer the turf creeps in over the eye, and if nobody rakes it back, the eye opens. That's all. It is a very simple job. You rake, and you sing, and it does not wake.

topic_2.speaker: Tamsin Hounder
topic_2.text: The last scouring, a wolf came up out of the swallet on the south flank while we were on the eye. Not at us. Past us, looking up at the figure, like a dog looking at its master's window. Aldous went after it with his rake and a cord tied to the lodge gate, because a scourer always ties on. The cord ran out. It never came back slack. It is still tight. I go and feel it.

topic_3.speaker: Tamsin Hounder
topic_3.text: He does. He knows every verse. — He is fifteen and he has his grandfather's legs and his grandfather's temper, and if I call them out he'll be the first up the Hound, and the first thing to come up that swallet will see him on the eye. I'll call them out when I know what's at the bottom of the cord. Not before.

hub.speaker: Tamsin Hounder
hub.text: Well?

choices.text: Why scour the Hound at all?
I'll go down the swallet and find what's on the end of the cord.
I've been to the bottom of the swallet.
Aldous's cord is on the gate.

bye.speaker: Tamsin Hounder
bye.text: Mind the eye if you go up the Hound. Don't stand in it long.

offer_the_eighth_summer.text: Will you. — Then go and look at the Hound first. Lie in the eye, where we sing it shut. See how far the turf has come in. Then go south to the swallet and follow the cord down, and bring me whatever is on the end of it. If it is Aldous, bring me his cord. If it is something else, bring me that.
offer_the_eighth_summer.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

accept_the_eighth_summer.text: Take a light. The Pelters go down there for wolf-skins, and they say it goes a long way down, and gets wider, which is never what you want a hole to do.
accept_the_eighth_summer.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

decide_the_eighth_summer.text: *(She takes the cord from you and runs it through her fingers to the knot at the rake-head, and does not say anything for a while.)* — Then he's found. And the thing he followed is dead, if you say so. — So. The eighth summer. Tell me what I ought to do, since you have been where I would not go.

choices.text: Call the scourers out. Rake the Hound white and sing the eye shut.
Let the turf have the eye. Whatever it kept asleep is dead.
Tie his cord on the gate. The seventy-second scouring was his.

decide_the_eighth_summer.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

decided_the_eighth_summer_scour.text: Then we scour. — Wat! Wat, get the carts. — The whole Vale will be up that hill tomorrow with rakes and pies, and I'll sing the eye four times, the way he did. Not because it didn't work. Because he'd want to hear it.
decided_the_eighth_summer_scour.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

decided_the_eighth_summer_let_it_grass.text: Let it grass. — My mother would have boxed your ears. My mother never went down the swallet. — I'll tell the Vale. Some of them will scour anyway, at night, when I'm not looking. I shall not look.
decided_the_eighth_summer_let_it_grass.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

decided_the_eighth_summer_tie_the_cord.text: The seventy-second. — Yes. He went down with a rake in his hand, singing. That was a scouring. It counts. *(She ties it on beside the others, a scourer's knot, and pulls it tight, and then lets it go slack.)*
decided_the_eighth_summer_tie_the_cord.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

after_scour.text: Every rake in the Vale. The eye's shut and white and you can see it from the Mere. Wat sang the eye verse. He only got the third one out on key. It'll do.
after_scour.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

after_grass.text: Green as a meadow from the knee down, and somebody has been up in the night and raked a white circle round the eye anyway. I didn't see who. I have very poor eyes, at night.
after_grass.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

after_cord.text: Seventy-two. People come and count them, and when they get to the last they stop and put a hand on it. I didn't ask them to. I didn't have to.
after_cord.speaker: Tamsin Hounder

notes: Tamsin Hounder's grandson at the Scourers' Lodge (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Wat Hounder
greet.text: You're not here to buy a rake. Nobody buys rakes. — Is she calling them out? Did she say?

topic_1.speaker: Wat Hounder
topic_1.text: You walk the Hound's outline in a line and sing a verse to each part: the nose, the ear, the back, the tail. Then everybody stands in the eye and sings it shut. Three times. Grandad sang it four, the last time. — I know all of it. I've sung it at the Hound from down here. It's not the same.

topic_2.speaker: Wat Hounder
topic_2.text: Wolves. The Pelters go down for skins, and they come up with skins and don't want to talk about it. One of them told me there's a lake at the bottom and a white thing lying by it that isn't a wolf and isn't a stone. Then his mate hit him.

topic_3.speaker: Wat Hounder
topic_3.text: I was on the tail! Then the eye. I was out of tune on the first two and nobody minded. Grandmother cried at the end, which she will say she didn't.

hub.speaker: Wat Hounder
hub.text: I've got nine rakes mended and a tenth that won't take a new head.

bye.speaker: Wat Hounder
bye.text: If you see a wolf up on the Hound, don't chase it. That's what Grandad did.

notes: The limeburner at the Lime Bay Kilns (hearthvale world life). Gives A Furrow Further Off: a season's quicklime to Rab Ashway.

greet.speaker: Hedda Limeburner
greet.text: Mind the draw-arch, it's hot enough to take your eyebrows. — You're looking at the cart. Everybody looks at the cart.

topic_1.speaker: Hedda Limeburner
topic_1.text: Everything. Merrowby whitewashes every wall at Candle Night so the windows show brighter. Tamwick sweetens its orchards. The cob in every house in the Vale is chalk and straw and my lime. — And the south farms lime their headland on the grey side every spring. They say it keeps the grey off. I don't say anything. I burn it.

topic_2.speaker: Hedda Limeburner
topic_2.text: Because Col won't take it and I can't leave the kilns. A bristleback came up out of the ditch at him by the Hare and Hurdle in spring and put a tusk through the near wheel. He's not a coward. He's nineteen and he saw a boar's eye very close. — The lime is sitting on that cart going stale, and Rab Ashway has the grey lying in his last furrow, and I am not saying those two things have anything to do with each other.

topic_3.speaker: Hedda Limeburner
topic_3.text: Col told me. He says Rab stood in the furrow with a shovel and cried, and then told Col he had lime in his eye. — Good. It's burnt lime. It'll do what it does, whatever that is.

hub.speaker: Hedda Limeburner
hub.text: What can I burn for you?

choices.text: Why hasn't the south cart gone?
Rab Ashway has limed his headland.

bye.speaker: Hedda Limeburner
bye.text: Tell anybody going south the kilns are drawing. They'll know what it means.

offer_a_furrow_further_off.text: Would you. — It's not the whole cart; nobody but a carthorse could. The first sack is the one that matters, Rab says: the headland first, then the field. Take the double sack with the red cord and give it to Rab Ashway himself, down past the Hare and Hurdle where the Vale stops. Keep it dry. Quicklime and rain are not friends.
offer_a_furrow_further_off.speaker: Hedda Limeburner

accept_furrow.text: If you meet a bristleback, a tree. Col will tell you: a tree, and not the one the boar is looking at.
accept_furrow.speaker: Hedda Limeburner

back_with_word.text: *(She hears it all with her hands in her apron.)* — Then it's done. The grey's a furrow off or it isn't, and either way the Ashways have their lime and it isn't sitting on my cart. Here. It isn't much. Lime doesn't pay; it only lasts.
back_with_word.speaker: Hedda Limeburner

notes: Hedda Limeburner's son at the Lime Bay Kilns (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Col Limeburner
greet.text: Oh — you're not a boar. Sorry. You came from the cut. Everything comes from the cut.

topic_1.speaker: Col Limeburner
topic_1.text: Bristleback. Out of the ditch by the Hare and Hurdle, no noise, and the near wheel went and I went off the back of the cart into the lime. It stood and looked at me. They give you one warning, the bristles going up. I saw the bristles go up. Then I was in a tree and I don't remember how.

topic_2.speaker: Col Limeburner
topic_2.text: Flint in the chalk bursts in the kiln and spoils the burn. So I pick it out, and the flint goes to the knappers at the Flint Pits and they make it into walls, and the lime goes into the walls between the flints. Everything in the Vale is chalk and flint. We just take them apart and put them back.

hub.speaker: Col Limeburner
hub.text: I pick the flint out. Somebody has to.

choices.text: What happened on the south road?

bye.speaker: Col Limeburner
bye.text: If you go south, the ditch by the Hare and Hurdle. Watch the ditch.

notes: The Table-Warden at the Brow Long Table (hearthvale world life). Gives the Hurdwell Bell: a buried family bell stolen by the Larkbourne Boys' eastern gang.

greet.speaker: Oswen Bellsey
greet.text: *(A single soft ring of the handbell.)* There. Now the table knows you're here. — Sit, if you like. There's a place for everybody on the Roll, and one or two spare, for strangers. You'd be a stranger.

topic_1.speaker: Oswen Bellsey
topic_1.text: Harvest. Every farm on the Brow, Rookdown to Bramcombe, one table, end to end, on the crest where the wind can hear it. We eat, and I read the places, and nobody is left off. That's the point of it. Nobody is left off. The Vale is afraid of being forgotten, so once a year it sits down together in a line a hundred paces long and makes sure.

topic_2.speaker: Oswen Bellsey
topic_2.text: When a line ends, the family's bell is buried at the table's foot with its handle up, so on the day I can ring it for them and they are still at the table. Cadwell, Pennock, Tiler. Hurdwell, last. Anse Hurdwell died in thirty-nine with nobody after him. — The Hurdwell bell was dug up in spring. The hole's still there. I ring the air over it.

topic_3.speaker: Oswen Bellsey
topic_3.text: Somebody with a Larkbourne boot. The Boys' eastern gang in Hanging Coombe take boundary-bells off the hawthorns; they hang them in the trees down there, the whole coombe tinkles. I think they took ours not knowing what it was. I think if they'd known, they'd have taken it anyway. They were struck off the Roll too, you see. They know what a bell at the foot of a table means.

hub.speaker: Oswen Bellsey
hub.text: What do you want of the table?

choices.text: Why are there bells at the foot?
I'll fetch the Hurdwell bell back from Hanging Coombe.
Is the bell back in the ground?
The bell's hung at the table's head.

bye.speaker: Oswen Bellsey
bye.text: *(One ring.)* The table says go well.

offer_the_hurdwell_bell.text: Would you. — Hanging Coombe is in the hollow of Rook Wood, east and a little north of here. Four of them and whoever leads them. The bell's small, bronze, green from the ground, HURDWELL round the shoulder. Bring it to the table and I'll know what to do with it. I think I will. Ask me when you're back.
offer_the_hurdwell_bell.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

accept_hurdwell.text: *(One ring.)* That's for you. The table knows you've gone for it.
accept_hurdwell.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

decide_the_hurdwell_bell.text: *(He holds it in both hands and rings it once, and it rings a little flat, as they all do.)* — Anse. There you are. — Now. The table's foot, or somewhere better? I've had all spring to think about it and I've changed my mind every evening.

choices.text: Bury it again at the table's foot, where it belongs.
Hang it at the table's head. Let the Hurdwells sit at the top for once.
Bury it, and ring it for the Boys too. They were struck off like the Hurdwells.

decide_the_hurdwell_bell.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

decided_the_hurdwell_bell_rebury.text: At the foot. With the handle up, so I can ring it. *(He kneels and puts it back in its hole and presses the turf round it with his thumbs.)* The line's ended. The table remembers. That's what the foot is for.
decided_the_hurdwell_bell_rebury.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

decided_the_hurdwell_bell_hang.text: At the head! — Anse would have hated it. He never once sat higher than the salt. — Yes. For one harvest. Then we'll see.
decided_the_hurdwell_bell_hang.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

decided_the_hurdwell_bell_ring_for_the_b.text: For the Larkbourne Boys. *(A long pause.)* The Roll says they're nobody's. The Roll isn't the table. — I'll ring it twice, then: once for the Hurdwells, and once for whoever they were before they were the Boys. If anybody at harvest asks what the second ring is for, I'll tell them it's for the people who took the bell. That'll start a row. A table needs a row.
decided_the_hurdwell_bell_ring_for_the_b.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

after_rebury.text: At the foot with the others, handle up. I ring it every evening. It rings a little flat. They all do.
after_rebury.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

after_rehang.text: At the head, on a hawthorn stake. Rookdown's reeve sat under it at harvest and didn't know whose it was and was very proud of himself.
after_rehang.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

after_boys.text: Twice every evening. Somebody's been leaving things on the table at night. A turnip. A good knife. A milestone, once, which took some carrying. I don't ask.
after_boys.speaker: Oswen Bellsey

notes: The Bramcombe shepherd at the Bram Down Wheelhouse (hearthvale world life). Gives Counted Out (novel round): the Drovers' Pound's last flock, never counted out.

greet.speaker: Enid Drove
greet.text: Stand still. You're in the count. — Seven score and six. Now you can move.

topic_1.speaker: Enid Drove
topic_1.text: Because the flock moves and I go with it. You drag it up in spring behind a horse and you drag it down at shearing and in between it's the best house on the Brow. It's never been downhill of the Naming Well. From my step I can see the Hush. A shepherd who can see the Hush doesn't sleep, and a shepherd who doesn't sleep doesn't lose ewes.

topic_2.speaker: Enid Drove
topic_2.text: Every evening I count them into the hurdles and every evening I count them again, and there's one more. Never the same one. I've walked the fold with the lantern and looked in every face, and they're all mine. — She stands on the Hush side and looks at the hut. She doesn't bleat. I've stopped being frightened of her. I've started leaving the gate on that side open a hand's width. It seems polite.

topic_3.speaker: Enid Drove
topic_3.text: On the darkest nights, to the hurdles. They don't come in. They look at the extra one, and then they go. Make of that what you like. I've made a good deal of it, over forty summers, and none of it's any use.

hub.speaker: Enid Drove
hub.text: Well? I've ewes to watch and so have you, now you're here.

choices.text: Where does the extra one come from, do you think?
I've brought the drovers' tally out of the pound.

bye.speaker: Enid Drove
bye.text: Go round the flock, not through it.

offer_count.speaker: Enid Drove
offer_count.text: I know where. I was nine. My father penned nine score Brow ewes in the Drovers' Pound the last night on Vale ground, and burned the count in on the board inside the gate, and word came up from the Southgate Stone that the Briar had shut. We'd take them home in the morning. -- In the morning there was fog to your knees and not a ewe in the pound, and the gate still barred. Nobody counted them out. Nobody could. -- The wolves have the pound now. If somebody brought me that board, I'd know what to do. Or I'd find out.

choices.text: I'll get the board out of the pound.

accept_count.speaker: Enid Drove
accept_count.text: Inside the gate, nailed to the post at a man's eye. Mind the wolves. They've had it fifty years and they think it's theirs. So does the down.

decide_count.speaker: Enid Drove
decide_count.text: *(She holds the board a long time, and runs her thumb along her father's burnt notches.)* -- Nine score and four, counted in at dusk. -- And no line for the morning. -- Well. You fetched it. I'll do it with you, if it's to be done. Or we leave it. Say.

choices.text: Count them out, with her, and burn the line in under the last.
Leave them counted in. The down has kept them this long.

decided_out.speaker: Enid Drove
decided_out.text: *(She heats the crook's iron in the stove and burns the line in herself, slow, saying the count aloud, nine score and four, and at the end of it: counted out.)* -- There. -- Go round the flock on your way down. Count them if you like.

decided_in.speaker: Enid Drove
decided_in.text: *(She hangs the board on a nail inside the wheelhouse door, where she can see it from her bed.)* -- In, then. Let the down keep them. It's kept me. -- She can stay, the extra one. I'd miss her.

after_out.speaker: Enid Drove
after_out.text: Seven score and six, and seven score and six. Two counts the same, the first time in forty summers. -- I didn't think I'd mind. I left the gate on the Hush side open a hand's width anyway.

after_in.speaker: Enid Drove
after_in.text: Seven score and seven, the second time. Always. She stands on the Hush side and looks at the board through the door. I tell her the count. She seems to like it.

notes: A Warden at Briarfoot Watch (hearthvale world life). Gives The Third Hand (novel round): the third hand on the tally-board, Amis Hale's bell, and her name to the Candle-Wheel.

greet.speaker: Ferris Oakden
greet.text: Warden Oakden, Briarfoot. The gate is shut, the thorn is across it, and the grey is a stride off the Southgate Stone. That is the whole of the news and I've said it now.

topic_1.speaker: Ferris Oakden
topic_1.text: Because a gate nobody watches is not a gate, it is a hole with a door in it. The Briar shut its gates in my grandfather's time and the Rest has kept a watch on every one since. The Woodfolk keep a watch on the other side. We watch each other watching. It's the longest conversation in Wickmere, and nobody has said a word in it.

topic_2.speaker: Ferris Oakden
topic_2.text: Neither of us. It says the grey is not coming to the Stone, it is coming to the tower, and to ask who is on the terraces at midnight. — I know who is on the terraces at midnight. So do you, if you've walked past the Southcote lynchets after dark. What I do not know is who told us.

topic_3.speaker: Ferris Oakden
topic_3.text: At midnight, when the singing's loud on the Brow, something comes up out of the grey to the foot of the tower and stands there. We bar the door. It goes by morning. Coppin wants to look. I've told her the Rest pays us to watch the gate, not the wall.

hub.speaker: Ferris Oakden
hub.text: Anything to report? We write it down.

choices.text: Why watch a gate that never opens?
Who chalked the line on the board?
What comes to the tower wall?
I'll be at the wall at midnight, and find out whose hand it is.
This bell lay under the tally-board.
Amis Hale's name has gone to the Candle-Wheel.

bye.speaker: Ferris Oakden
bye.text: If you're going to the Brow, go by day.

offer_hand.speaker: Ferris Oakden
offer_hand.text: At midnight. -- The Rest pays me to watch a gate, not a wall, and Coppin's twenty-three. But a Warden doesn't leave a line on a tally-board unanswered; that's the whole of what we are. Somebody chalked that line kneeling, at the tower's foot, in a hand I've never seen. Be at the foot when the thing comes up, and see what's left at the board in the morning. I'll be on the stair.

accept_hand.speaker: Ferris Oakden
accept_hand.text: I'll write it down that you went. If you don't come up the stair in the morning, I'll write that down too.

the_bell.speaker: Ferris Oakden
the_bell.text: *(He turns it over and reads the lip, and goes very still.)* -- AMIS HALE, BRIARFOOT. -- A Warden's bell, wired for the watch. *(He takes the Roll's copy from his coat and runs a finger down Briarfoot's page, and down it again.)* -- There's no Amis Hale. There's a gap. The year the gate shut, the page has a gap in it, a line's width, as if a name had been written and taken back. -- She stayed at the wall. That's who's been chalking. She's still keeping the watch, and the Roll let her go. -- The Dippers at the Candle-Wheel keep a candle for every name on the Roll. Take her name to them. It's the nearest thing to the Roll I can give her from here.

after_hand.speaker: Ferris Oakden
after_hand.text: The board's had nothing on it but our two hands since. I've hung her bell inside the door, wired. Coppin says good night to it. I don't. I say report.

notes: A Warden at Briarfoot Watch (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Jessamy Coppin
greet.text: Oh! Hello. Sorry. You're the first person from the Vale side in nine days. Ferris doesn't count. He does count, he counts everything, I mean he doesn't talk.

topic_1.speaker: Jessamy Coppin
topic_1.text: Every evening. I saw three of them on the far side of the thorn in the third week, at dusk, just standing, looking at the tower. I waved. They didn't. I've waved every evening since. I think if you wave long enough somebody has to wave back, or else they have to decide not to, and deciding not to is a sort of answer too.

topic_2.speaker: Jessamy Coppin
topic_2.text: The Wold, and Woodfolk, and the Hollow at the end of the road. Carts used to go east through it with Vale cider and come back with oak and honey. Ferris says the Briar shut because of something on the Vale side, not theirs. He won't say what. I've asked the Southgate Stone. It doesn't say either.

topic_3.speaker: Jessamy Coppin
topic_3.text: At midnight. When the thing comes to the wall. Ferris sleeps through it, or pretends to. I sit on the stair with my back to the door and listen to it breathe. It breathes like a man who's been working a field all day. — Then in the morning it's gone and the grey's a stride off the Stone and I wave at the Briar.

hub.speaker: Jessamy Coppin
hub.text: Have you been in the Briar? Have you seen them close to?

bye.speaker: Jessamy Coppin
bye.text: If you see anyone on the far side of the thorn — wave. For me.

notes: The grafter at the Mother Pippin (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Russet Graft
greet.text: Mind her arm, you're standing on it. — That limb there, along the ground: that's her. She lay down in a gale before anybody's grandmother, and where she touched the ground she put down roots and went on. Every apple in Wickmere is her child. Every one.

topic_1.speaker: Russet Graft
topic_1.text: Because she's here, and her children won't take anywhere else. The Ridgeways tried on the Wold side of their house and nothing took. The Woodfolk say their oaks won't have her. Tamwick says the Toll's fall made the Vale soft enough for her. I think she simply likes it here. So do I.

topic_2.speaker: Russet Graft
topic_2.text: A tree takes a lifetime to bear. You plant it for your grandchildren. The farms south of the Hare and Hurdle are the farms nearest the grey, and they are not sure they'll have grandchildren there. They don't say it. They say, kindly, apples are Tamwick's. — Aud Brow End took two once. They bear red. The Mother's children never bear red. Aud says it's the byre door.

topic_3.speaker: Russet Graft
topic_3.text: Bristlebacks. They come down to the windfalls at dusk and root under her and I go home, because a man with a grafting knife is not a thing a bristleback respects. They don't hurt her. They eat what she drops. She's fed the Vale for a thousand years; she can feed a boar.

hub.speaker: Russet Graft
hub.text: Would you like a scion? Everyone refuses. You could be the first.

choices.text: Why are apples only in the Vale?
Why won't the south farms take a scion?

bye.speaker: Russet Graft
bye.text: If you ever have a farm, come back for a scion. You'll have to wait a lifetime. It's worth it.

notes: The Wardens' Listener at the Listener's Shieling on the Brow (hearthvale world life). Gives What the Brow Sings: three verse-slates from the Hush Steps, Hushwatch and the Cliff Graves.

greet.speaker: Linnet Crale
greet.text: Shh — no. Sorry. It's gone. — I thought I heard the fourth voice. Come and sit, you'll hear it better sitting. Everything's louder close to the ground.

topic_1.speaker: Linnet Crale
topic_1.text: Verses. A few bars at a time, from nowhere in particular, under the wind, on still nights. Four voices, sometimes two, once a child's. They sing about keeping a note, and a door, and a table, and a lark. — The Roll says Larkstead was known for its singing. And in another hand, that they stopped. The Wardens keep a Listener up here because nobody at the Rest believes they stopped. Nor do I.

topic_2.speaker: Linnet Crale
topic_2.text: Because a thing written down is a thing somebody is keeping. The Vale knows that better than anyone. If Larkstead is singing and nobody is listening, it goes quiet the rest of the way. If somebody writes it down, it's in the Roll's company. It's the only thing I can do for them. I'm not brave. I'm a good listener.

topic_3.speaker: Linnet Crale
topic_3.text: When the singing's loud. The dead come up to hear it, I think. Not ours; the Hush's. I bar the door and listen through it. They don't do anything. They stand. I'd stand too, if I'd been dead a long time and somebody was singing.

hub.speaker: Linnet Crale
hub.text: Have you heard it? On the Brow, at night?

choices.text: Something comes up the cliff path at midnight.
I'll go to the three places and bring back what I hear.
Did the Rest take the verses?

bye.speaker: Linnet Crale
bye.text: Listen on your way down. You'll hear the larks by day. They're not the same, but they're kin.

offer_what_the_brow_sings.text: Oh — would you? — The three places it's loudest: the last of the Hush Steps, down the cliff face; between the Hushwatch stones on the lip of the Brow; and among the cliff graves above Rookdown. The Listener before me left a slate in each, for anyone who hears a verse there to chalk it down. They'll have been written on since. Bring me all three and I'll fill my pages.
offer_what_the_brow_sings.speaker: Linnet Crale

accept_brow.text: Go by day if you can. The slates don't mind. — And if you hear them singing while you're there, stand still and let them finish. It's only manners.
accept_brow.speaker: Linnet Crale

decide_what_the_brow_sings.text: *(She reads the three slates twice, moving her lips, and then a third time, singing under her breath, and stops.)* — They know we're listening. That one — 'we did not stop, we went on singing where nobody was listening' — that's to me. That's to the Wardens. — What should I do with them?

choices.text: Send them to the Rest. Let the Wardens write Larkstead's verses into the Roll.
Sing them back from the Brow. Let Larkstead hear someone answer.
Keep them in your book. Some things should be kept, not told.

decide_what_the_brow_sings.speaker: Linnet Crale

decided_what_the_brow_sings_to_the_rest.text: Into the Roll. Under Larkstead, in the other hand's place. The Wardens will argue for a month about whether a verse counts as a name. It does. — I'll send them down with the next dove from Hatchmoor.
decided_what_the_brow_sings_to_the_rest.speaker: Linnet Crale

decided_what_the_brow_sings_sing_back.text: Sing them back. *(She laughs, frightened.)* I haven't sung in front of anyone since I was nine. — Tonight, then. At the shieling door. If you hear a fifth voice on the Brow, it's me, and I'm out of tune, and I don't care.
decided_what_the_brow_sings_sing_back.speaker: Linnet Crale

decided_what_the_brow_sings_keep_listeni.text: Kept. — Yes. The Rest would turn them into an argument, and a song would turn them into a festival. My book's only a book. It'll keep them the way they were said.
decided_what_the_brow_sings_keep_listeni.speaker: Linnet Crale

after_rest.text: The Rest wrote back. The Roll-Warden has put the three verses under Larkstead's name, and under the words 'they stopped', in his own hand: 'not yet'.
after_rest.speaker: Linnet Crale

after_sing.text: I sang them every night for a week. On the eighth night, when I stopped, somebody finished the verse for me. From the Hush side. On key.
after_sing.speaker: Linnet Crale

after_keep.text: Every night. Three hundred and three verses. I'm not frightened of the pages any more. Only of the night they stop.
after_keep.speaker: Linnet Crale

notes: The carter's widow at the Wheel Graves (hearthvale world life). Gives The Other Ink: Captain Wendle's tithe book, and what it says about the carters.

greet.speaker: Bel Axtree
greet.text: Stand off the graves, please. — Thank you. People walk across them. They don't mean anything by it. The down doesn't look like a graveyard.

topic_1.speaker: Bel Axtree
topic_1.text: Five carters who would not pay a mark a wheel to the man in Scathe. Cob Ferrier. The Pennock boy. Ide Wheeler. A Woodfolk carter nobody knew. And Tom. — The carters who did pay buried them here, in sight of the fort, so the captain would have to look at them every day. They were ashamed. It was the only thing they could do and they did it.

topic_2.speaker: Bel Axtree
topic_2.text: A carter's wheel is his name in the Vale. You know a carter by his wheel before you see his face: the way it runs, the sound it makes on the flint. So you bury him with it standing up, and anybody going by knows what he was. — Tom's runs a little to the left. It always did.

topic_3.speaker: Bel Axtree
topic_3.text: His name out of that book. Wendle writes everybody down, in a careful hand, and the ones who wouldn't pay in a different ink, with what was done and who did it. Tom is in that book. I want it. — Whether I want to read it, I haven't decided. I've had all summer.

hub.speaker: Bel Axtree
hub.text: They were carters. Say what you've come to say.

choices.text: I have the captain's tithe book.
You read the names at the graves.

bye.speaker: Bel Axtree
bye.text: Walk round them, not across.

offer_the_other_ink.text: *(She looks at you a long time.)* — He keeps it in the keep, under the fort, where the Wardens kept their books. He'll not give it you. You'll have to take it off him, and he'll not give that either. — If you do, bring it here first. Not to the Rest. Here. Tom's owed that.
offer_the_other_ink.speaker: Bel Axtree

accept_other_ink.text: Third wheel from the end. That's where I'll be.
accept_other_ink.speaker: Bel Axtree

decide_the_other_ink.text: *(She takes the book in both hands and doesn't open it.)* — Five of them in the other ink. I can see it through the edge of the pages, the different colour. — Tell me what to do with it. I've decided four different things since you went, and I can't trust any of them.

choices.text: Read the other ink aloud at the graves, every name, what was done and who did it.
Burn it. Let what was done go with the man who wrote it down.
Send it to the Wardens' Rest, so the ones who did it answer for it.

decide_the_other_ink.speaker: Bel Axtree

decided_the_other_ink_read_aloud.text: *(She opens it. She reads it standing, to the wheels, in a carter's voice, the whole of it. It takes a long time. At Tom's name her voice doesn't change at all.)* — There. They've heard it. They know I know. — Now the down knows, too.
decided_the_other_ink_read_aloud.speaker: Bel Axtree

decided_the_other_ink_burn.text: *(She tears the pages out one at a time and burns them on the flint by the first wheel, and does not read one, though her eyes go to them.)* — It's his book. It was never theirs. Let it go with him.
decided_the_other_ink_burn.speaker: Bel Axtree

decided_the_other_ink_to_the_wardens.text: To the Rest. — Yes. The Wardens posted the bounty; they can read the other ink out in their yard and see who shuffles. Some of those names in the ordinary ink will be at the Long Table this harvest. Let them sit there knowing it's been read.
decided_the_other_ink_to_the_wardens.speaker: Bel Axtree

after_read.text: I read it to them every Tollday now. Not all of it. Just the names. The carters coming by the fort road stop and take their caps off.
after_read.speaker: Bel Axtree

after_burn.text: Ash on the flint, and the rain had it. I don't know what was done to Tom and I'm glad of it most days.
after_burn.speaker: Bel Axtree

after_wardens.text: The Wardens read the other ink in their yard. Two carters from Tamwick haven't come to the Long Table this year. Nobody's asked why. Everybody knows.
after_wardens.speaker: Bel Axtree

notes: The old roadman at the Roadmen's Lodge (hearthvale world life), great-uncle to the Larkbourne Boys.

greet.speaker: Abel Larkbourne
greet.text: If you're from the Wardens, the tea's stewed. If you're not, it's still stewed, but you can have some.

topic_1.speaker: Abel Larkbourne
topic_1.text: The crew's lodge. My great-great-grandad was ganger of the crew that laid the Vale's first roads, the year the Toll fell. Ninety days' work, and then the bell was down and the roads were laid and there was nothing else to lay. They were paid off at that table. Every man paid in full. Then the Wardens struck them off the Roll, because a crew with no road is nobody's neighbour. That's the Vale for you. Tidy.

topic_2.speaker: Abel Larkbourne
topic_2.text: Once a year. After dark. They stand in the yard and say their own names to the pay-table, one by one, because the pay-book has every name in it and not one struck, and it's the only book in the Vale that'll have them. Then they go back to robbing carts. I stay in my room. It's their table. — I'd be grateful if you didn't fight them in my yard. They're the only family I've got that visits.

topic_3.speaker: Abel Larkbourne
topic_3.text: To be talked about. Nobody remembers the Larkbourne Boys, and that's the whole grievance. You rob a man on the Merrowby road and he goes home and tells his wife it was the Larkbourne Boys, and there you are, in somebody's mouth, alive. It's a stupid way to be remembered. It's the only one the Vale left them.

hub.speaker: Abel Larkbourne
hub.text: Sit on the table if you like. Everybody else does, once a year.

choices.text: Why do they rob the roads?

bye.speaker: Abel Larkbourne
bye.text: If you meet any of them on the road, tell them their great-uncle says wipe their boots.

notes: The kennel-master at the Wardens' Kennels (hearthvale world life). Gives Nine Couple of Hounds: the Rest's pack gone to the wolves, by the Warden Barrow and Wolf Holt.

greet.speaker: Garrick Coupler
greet.text: Kennel's shut. — You've seen the chain. It's on the outside. That's not an accident.

topic_1.speaker: Garrick Coupler
topic_1.text: Gone. Three nights ago at midnight, nine couple over a six-foot wall without one of them giving tongue. Eighteen hounds. I've never known a hound go quiet on a line. They go quiet when they've been called by something they'd sooner hear than me.

topic_2.speaker: Garrick Coupler
topic_2.text: So that if they come back they find it shut, and they know it was them that left, not me that let them go. A hound has to know which. — And so I don't open it in the night when I hear them. I've heard them. Twice. Out on the down, west, giving tongue at last, and the wolves with them.

topic_3.speaker: Garrick Coupler
topic_3.text: Finding the lost. Somebody walks off the down in a mist, the Rest sends a couple out with the kennel's scarf of theirs to smell, and the hounds bring them home. We've brought home four hundred people in my time. We've never brought home a quiet-villager. The hounds won't take the line. They sit down in the road and look at me.

hub.speaker: Garrick Coupler
hub.text: What do you want?

bye.speaker: Garrick Coupler
bye.text: If you hear hounds on the down at night, don't answer them.

offer_nine_couple_of_hounds.text: *(He looks at the chain, not at you.)* — The Rest's Wardens say the pack was seen lying on the Warden Barrow the first night, round the kerb, where the first Wardens are. Start there. They'll have left something. Then west to the Holt; that's where the calling came from. Bring me back what you find. If you find Bellmouth, bring me her collar. I'll know from the collar.
offer_nine_couple_of_hounds.speaker: Garrick Coupler

accept_hounds.text: The wolves at the Holt won't give you the pack. Don't ask them nicely.
accept_hounds.speaker: Garrick Coupler

decide_nine_couple_of_hounds.text: *(He turns the collar over. He takes the twist of grass out of the bell and it rings, and he flinches.)* — Stopped. Somebody stopped her bell, so the pack couldn't hear where she was, so they'd follow the other call. — They're out there with the wolves now, the whole nine couple. — What would you do?

choices.text: Take the chain off. Leave the gate open. They'll come home if they want to.
The pack is lost. Breed a new one from the Rest's pups.
Let Pim call them home by name, every one, from the wall.

decide_nine_couple_of_hounds.speaker: Garrick Coupler

decided_nine_couple_of_hounds_open_the_g.text: *(He unhooks the chain and throws it in the grass.)* Open. — If they come, they come. If they don't, they had a better master. I'll sit here with the gate open and find out which I was.
decided_nine_couple_of_hounds_open_the_g.speaker: Garrick Coupler

decided_nine_couple_of_hounds_breed_agai.text: From the Rest's bitches. Two couple of pups this spring, and Pim to name them. — It'll take ten years to make a pack. It took the Rest a thousand to make that one. — Fine. We start.
decided_nine_couple_of_hounds_breed_agai.speaker: Garrick Coupler

decided_nine_couple_of_hounds_let_pim_ca.text: *(A long silence.)* — She's been doing it every night. I told her to stop. — Pim! Pim, come here. The gate. — *(He takes the chain off himself.)* Go on. All of them. In order.
decided_nine_couple_of_hounds_let_pim_ca.speaker: Garrick Coupler

after_open.text: Open. Seven of them are back. They came in one at a time, at dawn, and lay down by the trough as if they'd never left. Bellmouth isn't one of them.
after_open.speaker: Garrick Coupler

after_pups.text: Two couple of pups, and Pim's named every one, and every name is one of the old pack's. I haven't the heart to tell her you're not supposed to.
after_pups.speaker: Garrick Coupler

after_pim.text: She called them for nine nights. On the tenth, Old Sorrow came in over the wall, the way she went out. Then Ruby. Then the rest, one a night. Not Bellmouth. — Pim still calls her. Last, every night.
after_pim.speaker: Garrick Coupler

notes: Garrick Coupler's daughter at the Wardens' Kennels (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Pim Coupler
greet.text: Have you seen a hound? A big one with a bell? Her name's Bellmouth. If you've seen her, you'd know. She'd look at you like you were late.

topic_1.speaker: Pim Coupler
topic_1.text: Bellmouth. Ruby. Rake. Old Sorrow. Tansy and Tuck. Hollin. Merry and Moth. Ashby and Ash. Grip. Lark. Pepper and Pie. Wend. Toll. — That's eighteen. I say them every night so they don't forget them. Hounds don't forget their names. But you never know.

topic_2.speaker: Pim Coupler
topic_2.text: Something called them. I heard it. It wasn't the wolves, the wolves were calling too but this was under the wolves. Like somebody singing a hound's call who'd learned it from a long way off. — Da says don't talk about it. So I'm telling you, because you're not Da.

hub.speaker: Pim Coupler
hub.text: I leave them scraps. Da says not to. I do anyway.

bye.speaker: Pim Coupler
bye.text: If you see Bellmouth, tell her Pim's got her bowl.

notes: The bee-keeper at the Rookdown Bee-Garth (hearthvale world life). Telling the bees is a touch at the garth's bench (hearthvale.gd bee_garth).

greet.speaker: Tibby Wax
greet.text: Slowly, slowly. They like slow. — *(to the skeps)* It's a stranger, my loves, a stranger come up the down. *(to you)* There. Now they know. You can come in.

topic_1.speaker: Tibby Wax
topic_1.text: Because they leave if you don't. Every hive in the Vale's been told every birth and death since there were hives. Put a black ribbon on the skep for a death, and tell them who, and they stay. Forget, and they swarm off after a better-informed village. — Rookdown's bees have never swarmed. We tell them everything. Nearly everything.

topic_2.speaker: Tibby Wax
topic_2.text: The grey on the green. It's reached the well. I've sat on that bench three evenings with it in my mouth, and I can't. They'd take it badly from me; they know I'm frightened. — A stranger could tell them. Somebody who means it and doesn't have to live with it. They'd take it better. You could sit on the bench. Only if you want.

topic_3.speaker: Tibby Wax
topic_3.text: *(She puts her hand flat on the nearest skep and listens.)* — They're humming. Not angry. Just thinking it over. Thank you. They'll stay. I'll stay, then.

hub.speaker: Tibby Wax
hub.text: Have you news for them? They'll want it.

bye.speaker: Tibby Wax
bye.text: *(to the skeps)* The stranger's going now, my loves. *(to you)* Go slow.

notes: The keeper of Ash Watch this nine days (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Coll Ferrant
greet.text: Warden Ferrant, Ash Watch, day six. Don't stand where I'm standing, you'll see what I see. Stand there. That's the Vale. Much better.

topic_1.speaker: Coll Ferrant
topic_1.text: Because on the tenth day you'd stop seeing it. You'd look out at the ash and the Choir and it'd be just the view, and the day you stop seeing it is the day it comes up the Glassbed and you don't light the beacon. So nine days. The first three you can't stop looking. The middle three you hate it. The last three you understand why they built the tower here.

topic_2.speaker: Coll Ferrant
topic_2.text: Somebody walking south. Slowly, with a light, the way a person walks who is not tired and not in a hurry. I watched an hour. They didn't turn round. I wrote it down. The keeper before me had written the same, on the same night, the year before.

hub.speaker: Coll Ferrant
hub.text: Anything walking up the glass bed?

choices.text: What was the light on the ash?

bye.speaker: Coll Ferrant
bye.text: If you're going down to the line, look back at the tower. Everybody does. I wave.

notes: The keeper of Hound Watch (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Morwen Dagley
greet.text: Hound Watch. You can see everything from the crown. I don't recommend it. — Wine? It's the Rest's. They send it because they're sorry.

topic_1.speaker: Morwen Dagley
topic_1.text: The Choir's heads, plain as teeth. The piers at the head of the Stair. The Vale from here to the Mere, and every house in it I know somebody in. When a window lights at dusk in Ashwell I know whose it is. When one doesn't, I know that too. That's the part they don't tell you.

topic_2.speaker: Morwen Dagley
topic_2.text: Out of the south flank of Hound Down, since the Long Table. They don't look at the tower. They look at the Hound, up on the hill, the way a dog looks at the door when it hears its name. I've told the Rest. The Rest told the Hounders. The Hounders haven't scoured. — I've a bell up here for exactly this and I don't know what to ring it for.

hub.speaker: Morwen Dagley
hub.text: Ask me what I've seen. It's the only question anybody ever asks.

choices.text: The wolves come up in fours.

bye.speaker: Morwen Dagley
bye.text: If you're going up the Hound, I'll watch you. It's the one thing I'm good for.

notes: The keeper of the Brow Beacon (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Edwy Marl
greet.text: Forty-one, forty-two — you've made me lose it. Forty. Call it forty. — Brow Beacon. What is it?

topic_1.speaker: Edwy Marl
topic_1.text: Once for the Toll humming. The Wardens' orders: the Toll hums, the line burns. The second I lit on my own, for the singing on the Brow. You could hear it over the wind from here, four voices, and I thought: if Larkstead's singing, somebody should light a light so they know where the Vale is. — The Rest wrote me a stiff letter. I kept it.

topic_2.speaker: Edwy Marl
topic_2.text: Shuts its doors. Bramcombe brings the flocks in. The Vale behind it lights candles in the windows like Candle Night, so that from here you see the whole line of it light up west, farm by farm. It's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen and I've seen it twice, and I'd give a good deal never to see it again.

hub.speaker: Edwy Marl
hub.text: The stack's at nine nights. It's always at nine nights.

choices.text: Why was it lit twice this spring?
What does Rookdown do when it burns?

bye.speaker: Edwy Marl
bye.text: Forty-one. Forty-two. Go well.

notes: The fire-keeper at the Cliff Hearth (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Dilly Rookwell
greet.text: Come to the fire, it's lit for anybody. That's what the rota says, if you read it right. My aunt says it's lit for the drowned. The Wardens say for the Foundlings. I say for anybody coming up from the Hush who needs to see a light.

topic_1.speaker: Dilly Rookwell
topic_1.text: Nobody knows. That's the point, I think. If you knew who it was for, you could stop when they came. — The Southcotes were painted off the rota when they left the Last Field, and then somebody painted them back on, smaller. I know who. It was me. They still come up for their night. They've nowhere to be but here, one night a month.

topic_2.speaker: Dilly Rookwell
topic_2.text: Not in my time. The old women say they used to, one every generation or so, walking up the cliff path with the grey still in their hair, and they'd come to this fire first because it was the first light. — You didn't come up the cliff path, did you. No. You'd have said.

hub.speaker: Dilly Rookwell
hub.text: Sit, if you're sitting. Stick on the fire if you're not.

choices.text: Have Foundlings come up from the Hush?

bye.speaker: Dilly Rookwell
bye.text: If you're out on the Brow after dark, look for the fire. It's always lit. It's me.

notes: A Woodfolk fletcher cutting grey thorn at the Grey End (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Hale Brakewood
greet.text: You're on the Vale side of the thorn. So am I, today. — Don't touch the grey. Not because it'll hurt you. Because you'll want to again.

topic_1.speaker: Hale Brakewood
topic_1.text: Arrows that don't miss. The Wold wants them and won't cut them, so they send me. — What nobody asks is what the arrow doesn't miss. It goes where it's meant to. It isn't always meant by the one who looses it. I say that to every hunter I sell to. Most of them buy anyway.

topic_2.speaker: Hale Brakewood
topic_2.text: The Briar's gates are shut on the Wold side too. There's a way along the cliff at the Grey End, where the thorn's dead and doesn't fall. Nobody on either side minds a fletcher. Nobody on either side wants to know what he's cutting.

topic_3.speaker: Hale Brakewood
topic_3.text: Ash-wights, out of the Hush, walking the cliff. I'm gone by dusk. I've cut here nine years and I've never once been here after dark, and I intend to be the first Woodfolk fletcher to die of being old.

hub.speaker: Hale Brakewood
hub.text: One shaft a day. I've cut today's.

choices.text: What comes up the cliff at night?

bye.speaker: Hale Brakewood
bye.text: If you ever want a grey shaft, don't.

notes: A shepherd at the Hurdle Fold (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Emmet Ewell
greet.text: Mind the lantern. — No, it's lit, I only mean mind it. The ewes need to see it. If you stand in front of it half the flock thinks the fold's moved.

topic_1.speaker: Emmet Ewell
topic_1.text: So the ewes know where the fold is in the dark. A ewe out on the down at night, lost, with wolves about, looks for the light and comes to it. Every fold on the Brow has one. From the Naming Stone on a clear night you can see them all, a line of little lights along the down, like a Long Table set for the flocks.

topic_2.speaker: Emmet Ewell
topic_2.text: After dark. They try the hurdles. They don't get in, mostly. — Enid up at the wheelhouse says she has one ewe too many every night. I've one too few. I haven't told her. I think we're counting the same ewe.

hub.speaker: Emmet Ewell
hub.text: Lambing's done. Now it's just keeping them.

bye.speaker: Emmet Ewell
bye.text: If you see a ewe on her own, send her to the light.

notes: The shepherd at the Dewpond Fold (hearthvale world life).

greet.speaker: Mab Dewhurst
greet.text: You'll be wanting to look at the pond. Everybody does. Go on. It's the same height it was when I was a girl, and the same height it'll be when I'm dead, and nobody's ever seen it go down or come up.

topic_1.speaker: Mab Dewhurst
topic_1.text: Nobody. That's the thing. Every other dew pond on the downs was dug and puddled by somebody's great-grandfather, and they'll tell you whose. This one was here. The flocks drink from it all summer, four hundred ewes, and it doesn't go down. The dew fills it, they say. I've sat up all night to watch the dew fill it. It didn't. It was just full.

topic_2.speaker: Mab Dewhurst
topic_2.text: The ewes drink it. I drink it. I've never been ill a day. — I'll tell you what I don't do. I don't look at my face in it after dark. My mother told me not to and she never said why and I've never been curious enough to find out, which I think is the right amount of curious for a shepherd.

hub.speaker: Mab Dewhurst
hub.text: The flock's fine. The pond's fine. It's always fine. That's what worries me.

bye.speaker: Mab Dewhurst
bye.text: Drink if you're thirsty. Don't look in it after dark.

notes: The knapper at Knappers' Deep (hearthvale world life, phase 2). Gives the Night Shift: the Boys in the upper galleries, the Fall, and the overman at the far face.

greet.speaker: Nell Knapper
greet.text: Mind the flakes, they'll go through a boot. — If you've come to buy floorstone, I've got squared and I've got knobbed. If you've come to buy it off the Boys cheaper, the ladder's there and I hope you fall.

topic_1.speaker: Nell Knapper
topic_1.text: Floorstone. The black flint, the good seam, a man's height under the wall-stone, the best in the Vale. Every flint-faced wall you've walked past from Merrowby to Rookdown came up that ladder. My grandmother sank the deep shaft. My father was overman of the night shift. I square what comes up and I sell it to the builders, and these two summers what comes up, the Larkbourne Boys dig and sell to the man at the Flint Pits for two marks the sack, and he sells it to the same builders for six.

topic_2.speaker: Nell Knapper
topic_2.text: Eleven winters back, in the thaw. The night gallery had been talking for a week, the chalk does that before it goes, and he was going to prop it in the morning. It came down between the shift and the shaft. Seven men and him. We dug for nine days. On the ninth day the chalk came down on the diggers, and the Wardens said enough, and capped the gallery, and the Vale had the shift's names read at the Long Table. — I didn't. I keep the lamp.

topic_3.speaker: Nell Knapper
topic_3.text: Every night, when the wind drops. Iron on chalk, from under the down: seven, and then one. That's the overman's count. You count your shift down the ladder, seven and you, and you count them up again. The Boys say it's the chalk settling. The Boys won't go past the Fall after dark, though, will they.

hub.speaker: Nell Knapper
hub.text: Well? I've a cart to fill.

choices.text: What happened to the night shift?
I'll go down and turn the Boys out of your galleries.
I've been to the far face.
They're at the hedge line now.

bye.speaker: Nell Knapper
bye.text: If you're on the down after dark and you hear knocking, don't knock back. They'll think you're coming.

offer_the_night_shift.speaker: Nell Knapper
offer_the_night_shift.text: Will you. — Then the Boys first: they've a camp in the first gallery and a big lad who does their talking, and while they're down there nobody honest will go down. Then — if you've the stomach — past the Fall. They've cut round it, the Boys, digging along the seam; there's a way through now that wasn't there when we dug. Whatever's at the far face, I want my father's tally. An overman counts his shift up the ladder. Somebody has to finish the count.

accept_the_night_shift.speaker: Nell Knapper
accept_the_night_shift.text: Take a lantern off the hook, they don't come to the dark. And mind your head in the drift, my grandmother was short.

decide_the_night_shift.speaker: Nell Knapper
decide_the_night_shift.text: *(She takes the tally-stick and turns it in the light, a notch at a time, moving her lips over the names, and stops at the ringed one for a long while.)* — Eight. He got to eight. — So. It's my Deep again, and it's theirs, and somebody has to say what's done with it. You've been where I couldn't go. Say.

choices.text: Cap the shaft. Let the shift lie where they worked.
Work the Deep again. The floorstone's the Vale's, not the Boys'.
Dig through the Fall and bring them up to the hedge line, with their picks.

decided_cap.speaker: Nell Knapper
decided_cap.text: Cap it. — Aye. Oak and turf over the collar, and the gin wheel off, and the board left where it is. I'll keep the lamp a while yet. Not because they need it. I'm used to it.

decided_reopen.speaker: Nell Knapper
decided_reopen.text: Then I'll have the Cresswell lads and the Dunns' cousins on the gin by the Long Table, and pay them what the Boys never paid anybody. We'll prop round the Fall and leave it be, and every shift goes down the ladder will be counted down and counted up, by me, out loud.

decided_bring_up.speaker: Nell Knapper
decided_bring_up.text: The Vale buries its own at the hedge line with their tools so they've something to be known by. — It'll take the summer, digging through. I'll ask at the Hare and Hurdle for hands. They'll come, for this. And I'll put him at the end of the row, so he can count them.

after_seal.speaker: Nell Knapper
after_seal.text: Quiet down there now. I still listen. Habit.

after_reopen.speaker: Nell Knapper
after_reopen.text: Eleven sacks yesterday, and every man up the ladder by dark. Seven and me, I count, though there's nine of them. Habit.

after_bring_up.speaker: Nell Knapper
after_bring_up.text: Eight picks at the hedge line on the Hare and Hurdle road. Folk leave flints on them. I didn't ask them to.

notes: Merrowby's bellwright at the Hum Stone (hearthvale world life, phase 2). Gives the Stone's Note: the diggers in the Builders' throat, the Digger-King and the crown band.

greet.speaker: Godwin Merrow
greet.text: — hm. Hm-mm. Sorry. If I stop I lose it. — You've walked out from Rookdown? Then you'll have heard it, coming up the field. Everybody hears it and nobody listens. That's the Vale for you.

topic_1.speaker: Godwin Merrow
topic_1.text: Merrowby keeps seventeen family bells, one a household of the first roll, and I keep them in tune, and my father before me. When the Toll began to hum this spring every one of them hummed with it, very faintly, in its tree. And the stone out here. I came to take its note, so I'd know what the Toll is trying to say. — And then the diggers started cutting its bands, and the Cresswells' bell cracked in the night. Then the Ashdowns'. One a band. You see why I'm out here and not at home with my feet up.

topic_2.speaker: Godwin Merrow
topic_2.text: Barrow-diggers. Larkbourne Boys who found the dead pay better than carters. Dunstan Spade's lot, him that opened Orm's barrow. They cut two bands off the stone with cold chisels, and then they found a door under it, one of the Builders' with no hinge, and they've been carrying bronze up out of it in sacks ever since. Except that for a fortnight nobody's come up. And the Hush's dead come up the cliff of a night instead, and stand on the grey side, and listen.

topic_3.speaker: Godwin Merrow
topic_3.text: I don't know what it's for. I'm a bellwright, not a Sayer. But I know what a bell is for. A bell is so that people know. Where you are, what's happened, who's dead, that it's time to come in. A bell nobody listens to is a lump of metal. — The Builders hung four bands on that stone and something at the bottom of it, and for two thousand years nobody listened. And now everybody is.

hub.speaker: Godwin Merrow
hub.text: Hm-mm. — Yes?

choices.text: I'll go down after the diggers and the bronze.
I've been to the bottom of the throat.
The bands are back on the stone.

bye.speaker: Godwin Merrow
bye.text: Be off the lip by dark. They don't do anything. They just stand. But they stand very close.

offer_the_stones_note.speaker: Godwin Merrow
offer_the_stones_note.text: Would you? — I'm no good under the ground, I'll tell you that for nothing, I get as far as the door and my knees go. Dunstan Spade's down there somewhere with the biggest band, the one off the crown, I'd stake my forks on it. Get it back from him. However you have to. Then come and tell me, and we'll decide what's to be done with it, because I've been out here a month and I still don't know.

accept_the_stones_note.speaker: Godwin Merrow
accept_the_stones_note.text: Listen as you go. If the hum gets louder you're going the right way. If it stops — hm. If it stops, come back up.

decide_the_stones_note.speaker: Godwin Merrow
decide_the_stones_note.text: *(He unrolls the band across his knees, and knocks it with one knuckle, and shuts his eyes while it rings.)* — Oh. Oh, that's the crown. That's the note the whole stone hangs on. — Right. Right. It's ours now, and nobody's told me what to do with a thing like this. You've been down. Tell me.

choices.text: Hang it back on the stone. Let it keep its note.
Take it to Merrowby. Cast an eighteenth bell out of it.
Bury it under the hump and let the stone go quiet.

decided_rehang.speaker: Godwin Merrow
decided_rehang.text: Back on the stone. — Yes. I'll need a ladder from Rookdown and a smith who isn't frightened of heights. And then everybody on the Brow can go on hearing it and not listening, the way they did for two thousand years. Somebody'll listen. I'll come out once a year. I'll bring the forks.

decided_cast.speaker: Godwin Merrow
decided_cast.text: An eighteenth bell. For no household. For — for the ones the Roll's lost, I suppose, if anyone asks, and they will. Hung in the oak by the Toll, where it can hear the Toll and the Toll can hear it. I'll cast it at midsummer. You'll come? You should be there when it's first rung. Somebody should know who brought it.

decided_quiet.speaker: Godwin Merrow
decided_quiet.text: Quiet. — Aye. The Order would say so, if any of them were left this side of the Ash. I'll bury it myself. And then I'll go home and see how many of my seventeen are still whole. — It'll be a strange thing, the Brow without the hum. I'd only just got used to it.

after_rehang.speaker: Godwin Merrow
after_rehang.text: Hm-mm. Hear that? Sharp again, near enough. The Ashdowns' bell's still cracked. But it hasn't cracked any further.

after_cast.speaker: Godwin Merrow
after_cast.text: Rings like a held breath. The Toll answers it, some nights. The Wardens don't like it. The Wardens didn't like the Toll humming either.

after_quiet.speaker: Godwin Merrow
after_quiet.text: No dead on the lip since. No hum. I keep humming it myself, out of habit, so I won't lose it. Somebody ought to have it.

notes: The lamp-keeper at Wake Barrow (hearthvale world life, phase 2). Gives The Long Wake: the stone walked out, the Ash Winter's dead and Ebba Crowle at the bottom with her lamp gone out.

greet.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
greet.text: One, two, three. — You came up by the coffin-rests. Did you leave a coin? Everybody used to. Nobody's been carried up here in two hundred years and they still leave a coin, and I take them down to Pilgrims' Ash and buy oil. That's the whole of my living, near enough. That and the sheep.

topic_1.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
topic_1.text: The Ash Winter. The Vale couldn't bury its dead because it couldn't dig, and couldn't feed itself, and the dead came up the down in carts. Ebba Crowle was barrow-wife. A barrow-wife sits three nights with each of the dead, so they know they're dead and go easy. There were hundreds. She went down with all of them and her lamp, and had the stone rolled across, and told them up top to keep a lamp in the niche so she'd know they were still alive up here. — And we have. Every night. Two hundred years.

topic_2.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
topic_2.text: Since midsummer the lamp's been out every morning. Oil in it. Wick fine. Out. And every morning the stone's a hand further out of its socket, as if something were leaning on it from inside, very patiently. Now there's room to get by it. Now they come out of a night, two or three, and stand at the tail looking down the Vale, like folk waiting for a cart. I bar my door.

topic_3.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
topic_3.text: The oaks? Seven. Planted by the barrow-wives on the barrow's back, one for every wife that sat the wake, so the Vale could see from anywhere where its dead were. You can see them from the Pilgrims' road and the Brow and Hound Watch. Ebba's is the one at the face end. It's dying. It's been dying since midsummer.

hub.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
hub.text: One, two — sorry. Yes?

choices.text: I'll go down and see what's leaning on the stone.
I've been to the bottom of the barrow.
Did the Wardens come for her?
I'll leave you to your lamp.

bye.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
bye.text: Leave a coin on the way down. It's not for me. It's for her.

offer_the_long_wake.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
offer_the_long_wake.text: Would you. — I've been to the stone a dozen times this summer and got as far as the dark and no further. I'm a Crowle; I ought to. But I'm a Crowle who's never sat a wake, and they'd know. — She had her lamp with her. If it's gone out down there, that's why ours goes out up here. Bring it up to me. Whatever's down there with it. Then we'll know what to do.

accept_the_long_wake.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
accept_the_long_wake.text: Take a light. Tell them your name if they ask. Don't eat down there. — And if you find her, tell her we're still alive up here. That's all she ever wanted to know.

decide_the_long_wake.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
decide_the_long_wake.text: *(She takes the lamp in both hands and turns it over, and touches the burnt wick, and doesn't say anything for a while.)* — That's hers. That's the one. — So she sat them all. Every one. And then there was nobody to sit with her. — It's ours to say now, isn't it, what's done. You've been down. Say.

choices.text: Light it again at the bottom, by her, and let the stone go back.
Take her name to the Wardens. Bring her up, and put her on the Roll.
Keep it in the niche, lit, and sit her wake up here yourself.

decided_relit.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
decided_relit.text: Back down by her. Lit. — Yes. I'll fill it and trim it and take it down myself, as far as the hall with the benches, and you'll take it the rest. And then we'll get the Pilgrims' Ash men up with ropes and lean the stone back. And I'll go on keeping ours up here, so she knows. Some things you don't stop.

decided_rolled.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
decided_rolled.text: The Roll. — A Crowle on the Wardens' Roll. My gran would have spat. But she'd have been wrong; Ebba kept the Vale's dead before there was a Rest to keep anybody, and it's past time somebody wrote her down. I'll walk to the Rest myself. They can send their men for her bones. The others — the others she sat with. They know now. They can stay.

decided_kept.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
decided_kept.text: Up here. In the niche. — I've never sat a wake. Three nights, the rules say. I'll do three nights for her, here at the face, with her own lamp, and tell her her name, and that she's dead, and who's still alive, and that it's all right. And then I'll do it again. A Crowle ought to.

after_relit.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
after_relit.text: Lit. The stone's back in its socket, near enough, and ours stays lit till morning. The oak at the face end has put out leaves again. In September. Don't tell me that's nothing.

after_rolled.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
after_rolled.text: Four Wardens and a handcart, and the Roll-keeper himself, walking. They wrote her in under the first year of the Roll, before anybody else. Ebba Crowle, barrow-wife. Nobody's come out of the barrow at night since.

after_kept.speaker: Tamsin Crowle
after_kept.text: Thirty nights now. I tell her the same every night. Some nights I think the lamp leans toward me instead of the barrow. — The coins have started again. People walking up from Pilgrims' Ash to leave one. I didn't ask them to.

notes: The cote-wife at the Letter-Cote (hearthvale novel round). No quest: the doves are sent from her table (core:dialogue/letter_cote_doves).

greet.speaker: Wenna Cotter
greet.text: News for the road! -- Oh, you're not the road, you're a person. Hello. Rookdown's bees are swarming, Ashwell's well is sweet again, and a Tamwick cow has had two calves and they're both called Hob. That's today. Have you any? I'll send it on.

topic_1.speaker: Wenna Cotter
topic_1.text: Every village keeps a pair of my birds in a basket. When there's news, they tie it on and let one go, and it comes home here, and I read it out on the road and send it on to whoever ought to hear. The Candle says a village that's talked of stays lit. So I talk. Seven hundred birds' worth of talking. It's a living.

topic_2.speaker: Wenna Cotter
topic_2.text: Mullbourne, Harewell, Larkstead and Gosford. Struck off the Roll Stone before I was born, because nobody could find the road to them any more. My mother wrote to them every week anyway, and so do I. Somebody ought to. The birds always came back, with nothing on their legs. -- Always. Until the spring.

topic_3.speaker: Wenna Cotter
topic_3.text: Since the spring, one in four comes back from Harewell with an answer. A child's hand. They're well, the barley's in, please keep writing. -- I don't know what it means. I know what my mother would have said. She'd have said: then keep writing. They're in the box by the door if you want to read them. Leave them where they are.

hub.speaker: Wenna Cotter
hub.text: Well? I've birds coming in.

choices.text: How do the doves carry the news?
Who do you write to that nobody else does?
I've read the letter from Harewell.

harewell.speaker: Wenna Cotter
harewell.text: *(She reads it again, though she must know it by heart.)* -- The fog goes back a bit. -- I'll write tonight. I'll tell them about you. That's two people talking about them now. Perhaps that's what it takes.

bye.speaker: Wenna Cotter
bye.text: Tell somebody something on the way. It's how the Vale stays where it is.

notes: The chandler at the Candle-Wheel (hearthvale novel round). A merchant (candles); the host of The Third Hand's last choice (Amis Hale's name). Candles are dipped for names at the vat (core:dialogue/candle_wheel_dip).

greet.speaker: Tallis Dipper
greet.text: Mind the vat; it's hotter than it looks and it looks hot. -- Candles? The Dippers dip the Vale's. All of it. Every window on Candle Night has one of ours in it, and every name on the Roll has one burning in the shed there.

topic_1.speaker: Tallis Dipper
topic_1.text: You walk it round. Dip, lift, walk the turn while they cool, dip again. Thirty dips makes a candle. My mother walked it, and hers, back six. It's not hard. You just can't stop. A candle that's let go cold between dips cracks, and then it's no use to anybody. -- The Candle says that's true of everything.

topic_2.speaker: Tallis Dipper
topic_2.text: The Wardens send for a new one each time a name's put on the Roll, and I send it, and they burn it in the Roll room at the Rest, and the twin of it burns on my shelf. None of mine has ever gone out. Not in six generations. Not one.

topic_3.speaker: Tallis Dipper
topic_3.text: One has. Three nights now. I light it at dusk, and in the morning it's out and cold and the name chalked under it's been scraped off the shelf, as if with a thumbnail. I thought it was a child. There aren't any children up here. -- I don't know whose it was. That's what frightens me. I knew every name on that shelf.

hub.speaker: Tallis Dipper
hub.text: Well? The wheel won't wait.

choices.text: What are the candles in the shed?
I've come about a name: Amis Hale, a Warden at Briarfoot.
Is Amis Hale's candle still lit?
Did the Rest write Amis Hale in?

amis.speaker: Tallis Dipper
amis.text: *(She stops the wheel. She has never stopped it in front of you before.)* -- Hale. A for Amis. -- That's it. That's the one. I had to read the scrape with my fingers: A, and a long stroke. A Warden. -- So the Rest forgot her and the candle didn't, and it's been going out to tell somebody. -- What do you want done? You brought the name.

choices.text: Dip her a new candle and set it on the shelf where the old one was.
Send her name to the Rest with the next Roll candles, to be written in.

decided_shelf.speaker: Tallis Dipper
decided_shelf.text: On the shelf, then, with her name chalked fresh, and I'll walk the wheel round for it myself. -- There. Look at that. It's leaning toward the south, toward the Briar. They do that, the ones for Wardens on a gate. They lean toward the gate.

decided_rest.speaker: Tallis Dipper
decided_rest.text: The Rest, then. I'll send her down with the Roll candles on Tollday and a letter to the Roll-keeper in my own hand, and they'll write her in, or they'll have me to answer. And I'll keep the twin on my shelf. She's had enough of going out.

after_shelf.speaker: Tallis Dipper
after_shelf.text: Lit every night, and leaning south. It hasn't gone out once. -- I've started saying her name when the wheel comes round. Every turn. I don't know why I never said it before; I suppose because I'd never heard it.

after_rest.speaker: Tallis Dipper
after_rest.text: They wrote her in. Under the year the gate shut: Amis Hale, Warden, Briarfoot, who stayed at the wall. The Roll-keeper sent me the line in his own hand. I've pinned it over her candle.

bye.speaker: Tallis Dipper
bye.text: Light something tonight. For anybody.

notes: The reeve of the Scarecrow Moot (hearthvale novel round). Gives The Forty-First.

greet.speaker: Abner Strawe
greet.text: Morning, Hurdlegate. Morning, Coldharbour. Morning, Ashway. -- And you. You're not a farm. Come and stand where they can see you; they like a new face.

topic_1.speaker: Abner Strawe
topic_1.text: Seven years in a field and a scarecrow's heard the farm's name said every morning of it. 'Up and out to Coldharbour top.' It knows. You don't burn a thing that knows your name; that's asking to be forgotten. So they come up here, and stand together, facing home, and the farm's still said somewhere. I say it. Forty farms, every morning.

topic_2.speaker: Abner Strawe
topic_2.text: Midsummer night, they say, the Moot talks. Every farm's news, all at once, like a market. I've stood out here thirty Midsummers and never heard it. -- I've heard the rooks go quiet, though, all of them at once, about midnight, and stay quiet an hour. You draw your own conclusions.

topic_3.speaker: Abner Strawe
topic_3.text: Forty. I set forty. It's on the post. I can name you every one and the farm it came from and who carried it up. This summer I walk the ranks of a morning and say forty names and there's one left over at the end of the third rank in a dead man's coat, and it doesn't answer to any farm. And the rooks won't sit on it.

hub.speaker: Abner Strawe
hub.text: Well? I've coats to mend.

choices.text: I'll find the one that doesn't belong.

offer.speaker: Abner Strawe
offer.text: Would you. I've walked up to it a dozen times with my needle and stopped a pace off. I'm too old to be brave about a thing I can't name. -- End of the third rank. Don't look at the coat; look under the hat. A scarecrow's got a sack for a face. Mind yourself if it hasn't.

accept.speaker: Abner Strawe
accept.text: I'll be at my trestle. If you shout, I'll come. Slowly.

done.speaker: Abner Strawe
done.text: A hedge-wight. Out of a Coldharbour hedge, I'd say, by the clay on it, and somebody's good coat on its back that it took off a line. Stood up here among them all summer facing Merrowby like it belonged, learning the farms. -- Forty, then. Morning, Hurdlegate. Morning, Coldharbour. -- Here. This was Coldharbour's hat. It's done its seven and its thirty and it'd sooner be on somebody who walks about. Take it.

after.speaker: Abner Strawe
after.text: Forty, every morning, and the rooks on every one. There's a new one coming up from Ashway next week in a red waistcoat. Forty-one, but the right kind.

bye.speaker: Abner Strawe
bye.text: Say the name of a farm on the way down. Any farm. They hear it.

notes: The watcher at Wassail Knap, Hob Applegarth's granddaughter (hearthvale novel round). Gives The Last Wassail.

greet.speaker: Pip Applegarth
greet.text: *(She knocks twice on the trunk beside her before she turns round.)* -- Don't go near the cellar-head. Whatever you've heard in Hazelcombe, don't. -- Sorry. You're not from Hazelcombe. I've been saying that to everybody for a month.

topic_1.speaker: Pip Applegarth
topic_1.text: Every Twelfth Night, for longer than the Roll, the East Downs came up the knap to wassail the orchard. You crown a King. You beat the trees with sticks to wake them, and put toast in their branches and cider on their roots, and sing. Then the King takes everybody down to the Mother Vat to wake her, the oldest cask in the Vale, and at dawn he gives the crown back up the stair. That's the rule. A King for one night.

topic_2.speaker: Pip Applegarth
topic_2.text: My grandfather, Hob Applegarth. Best King they ever had, everybody says. He wouldn't give it back. Said the singing was too good to stop and he'd stop it when it was finished. The press-master barred the door on him by the rules, and the whole wassail with him, and nobody's pressed an apple here since. My gran used to come up and listen at the grates. -- Forty years. She said you could still hear him.

topic_3.speaker: Pip Applegarth
topic_3.text: This spring every tree on the knap came into blossom in one night, at midnight, dead forty years. In the morning there was fresh toast in the Wassail Tree. The trees fruited the next week, blossom and apples on the same branch. Three of our pickers came up to pick it: Eddy, Joan and little Nat. They went down the stair after the singing at dusk. I watched them go. I didn't stop them. I couldn't hear anything but the singing.

hub.speaker: Pip Applegarth
hub.text: Well? Keep your back to the cellar-head; it helps.

choices.text: Who was the last Wassail King?
I'll go down after your pickers.
It's done. The crown's gone back.

offer.speaker: Pip Applegarth
offer.text: You'd go down. -- Then listen. Don't drink anything they give you. Don't dance, however good it is, and it will be good. Find Eddy and Joan and Nat. And if it's my grandfather keeping it going, he'll have the crown on, and if anybody gets it off him the singing stops and everybody can go home. -- Don't bring the crown to me. It was cut from the Mother Pippin's withies by Tamwick, that's the old rule, and it goes back to her, not to any Applegarth. Promise.

accept.speaker: Pip Applegarth
accept.text: Knock twice on the door before you open it. It's what you do. -- I'll be here. I'm always here now.

report.speaker: Pip Applegarth
report.text: *(She has been listening at the grates. She stands up slowly.)* -- It stopped at dusk. All at once, mid-verse, like somebody'd put a hand flat on a fiddle. And then I heard them coming up the stair, slow, and I thought, that's Eddy's cough. -- They're home. They're asleep in the Hazelcombe barn and they say they danced one night. -- Thank you. From the Applegarths. Both of us.

after_hung.speaker: Pip Applegarth
after_hung.text: Quiet down below. Up top -- look at it. The whole knap's in leaf, and the Mother Pippin by Tamwick has put out a second blossom, they say. I've started pruning. Somebody might press here again.

after_buried.speaker: Pip Applegarth
after_buried.text: Quiet. The blossom fell the next night, every petal at once, and the trees are bare again and sleeping, properly sleeping. I'll stay the winter, and then I'll go home. It's done.

after_tamwick.speaker: Pip Applegarth
after_tamwick.text: Quiet. Tamwick's got the crown on a hook behind the press-house door, and come Twelfth Night they'll crown somebody, and at dawn the somebody'll give it back, or Tamwick will know what to do about it now. -- They've asked me to be King. I said I'd think about it.

bye.speaker: Pip Applegarth
bye.text: Knock twice on a tree on your way. It costs nothing.

notes: The keeper of Tamwick Troy (hearthvale novel round). The ritual is the touch at the heart (core:dialogue/troy_heart).

greet.speaker: Maudie Twelvetrees
greet.text: Gate's open, the Troy's walked, mind the clippings. -- In all the way round and out all the way round. No stepping through the hedge. It knows.

topic_1.speaker: Maudie Twelvetrees
topic_1.text: Five rings and one way through each, so the way in goes round everything there is before it gets anywhere. A child walks it on Naming Day with its old name and comes back out with its new one, said at the pole. A name said at the heart can't be dropped on the way out, see, because you've already been all the way round.

topic_2.speaker: Maudie Twelvetrees
topic_2.text: Grown folk, these last years. They come at dusk from Merrowby and Ashwell and walk in with their own names, because they'd gone in the kitchen to fetch something and couldn't think what they were called. That's the grey, that is. It gets in at the edges. I stitch the name on a ribbon for them and tie it on the pole.

topic_3.speaker: Maudie Twelvetrees
topic_3.text: Somebody tied a ribbon with no name on it. I saw nobody walk in. I've walked it three times to see who's at the heart. -- Nobody. Only the ribbon, and the wind saying nothing in it. I've left it. You don't untie a ribbon at the Troy.

hub.speaker: Maudie Twelvetrees
hub.text: Walking it, or talking?

choices.text: What's the ribbon with no name?

bye.speaker: Maudie Twelvetrees
bye.text: Out all the way round, mind. Not through.

notes: The ganger of the figure-cutters at the Unfinished Figure (hearthvale novel round). The face is chosen at the touch core:dialogue/figure_face.

greet.speaker: Col Whitcut
greet.text: Mind the string. That's her candle arm you're standing on. -- Forty turves a day, us four, and she's eleven hundred turves tall. You do the sum. We'll be here till Candle Night.

topic_1.speaker: Col Whitcut
topic_1.text: A woman of Harewell, holding up a candle. The cote-wife at the Letter-Cote paid for her: seven years of dove money, three hundred turves of it. So the whole Vale sees Harewell from the Tamwick road every day and talks about it. Cutting's how the Vale keeps a thing. The Hound's kept a hound asleep two hundred years.

topic_2.speaker: Col Whitcut
topic_2.text: Her face. We peg it, we cut it, and in the morning the turf's back down on it, every turf, laid neat as a hedger's. Not dug back. Laid. -- Nobody can tell us what she looked like. Wenna says a woman of Harewell. Which woman? Nobody remembers a single face out of Harewell. You can't cut what nobody remembers. The down won't have it.

topic_3.speaker: Col Whitcut
