topic_3.text: Bristlebacks, at dusk, after the grubs under the lifted turf. Big as a cart. They don't mind us. They mind the turf. Stand off and let them root, or don't, and run.

hub.speaker: Col Whitcut
hub.text: Well? I'm losing turves standing here.

choices.text: Why is her face only string?

after.speaker: Col Whitcut
after.text: Cut, and it's stayed cut. Three mornings. The turf's not come back. -- I stood on the Tamwick road last night and looked up, and she was there, with her candle, looking down at the road, and I'll tell you a thing: I knew her. I don't know from where.

bye.speaker: Col Whitcut
bye.text: Look up from the road on your way. She's worth a look already.

notes: The rook-wife at the Witness Elms (hearthvale novel round). What the rooks show is at the stump (core:dialogue/witness_stump).

greet.speaker: Hester Corvey
greet.text: Get off, you. -- Not you. Him. -- You'll be wanting something seen. Leave a bright thing on the stump and stand still. And don't look at them straight; they don't like it.

topic_1.speaker: Hester Corvey
topic_1.text: Everything done on the downs, a rook saw. They don't forget, and they tell each other, and they tell me if I pay. That's why nobody in the Vale kills a rook: you'd be killing a witness, and the others would have seen you do it.

topic_2.speaker: Hester Corvey
topic_2.text: The Ash Winter killed the elms and the rooks wouldn't leave them. Two hundred years they've nested in dead wood. They say the rooks stayed because the elms saw it too, the winter, and somebody had to keep them company.

topic_3.speaker: Hester Corvey
topic_3.text: They bring me things now. That's new. A Warden's brass button, polished. A child's ring. A bell-clapper off a Merrowby bell. They put them on the stump and look at me. It's the wrong way round. -- They want something shown, and it's me that's meant to look, and I don't know where.

hub.speaker: Hester Corvey
hub.text: Well? They're watching you.

choices.text: What are the rooks bringing you?

bye.speaker: Hester Corvey
bye.text: Don't kill a rook on the way. They'd know by supper.

notes: Farmer at Southgate keeping watch at the Great Barn (hearthvale novel round, the second large site). Gives The Last Sheaf.

greet.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
greet.text: *(He bites a grain and spits the husk.)* -- Green. Green as grass. Somebody cut it a month early, and cut it well, and stood it up facing this barn. -- Who are you, then? Not a reaper. You've got clean hands.

topic_1.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
topic_1.text: The tithe barn. My grandfather was reeve of it. The East Downs brought their tithe sheaves here for the Briar carts. Then the Briar shut with the barn full to the purlins, and nobody would buy and nobody could eat it all, and the roof came in on it. Fifty years it's been rotting in the undercroft. You can smell it on a warm night. Sweet. Like a brewhouse.

topic_2.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
topic_2.text: The last sheaf of every harvest, plaited into a kern-baby with a crown on, and hung on the tie-beam all winter so the harvest's life is kept somewhere till spring. Plough Monday you carry her out and plough her into the first furrow and the harvest comes back. -- Grandfather hung her the year the Briar shut. Nobody carried her out. Nobody came back in spring at all.

topic_3.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
topic_3.text: Straw. Men of straw, walking out of the old ricks at dusk with hooks. I've seen two from the step. They cut what's growing, any of it, and stand it up facing the barn, like they're bringing in a harvest for somebody. The bristlebacks come out of the stair after them, fat as bishops.

hub.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
hub.text: Well? I've a field to watch.

choices.text: I'll go down the stair and see what's bringing the harvest in.
It's done. The kern-knot's gone where it belongs.

offer.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
offer.text: Would you. I've been down to the third step with a lantern and the straw on the stair moved. -- Grandfather's tally'll be in the tithe vault, if it's anywhere; he burned everything into it. Find that and you'll know what went on down there at the end. And if it's her, the Mother, still hanging -- she wants carrying out. That's all she ever wanted. Mind she doesn't decide it's you that's to be ploughed in.

accept.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
accept.text: Take a light and a torch both. Straw doesn't like fire, and I'd want it to know you had some.

report.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
report.text: *(He looks out at the top field a long time.)* -- Nobody's cut it since. It's standing. Green, but standing. -- Grandfather's tally had no mark for Plough Monday. I've burnt one in. Late, but in. -- Here. From the Southgates. We pay our tithe.

after_table.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
after_table.text: Standing, and the Long Table had the best harvest supper anybody on the Brow remembers, the kern-knot at the head of it. They've asked me to cut the last sheaf next year. I said yes before I'd thought.

after_furrow.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
after_furrow.text: I ploughed her into the first furrow myself, a month late, singing the old words badly. The top field's come up again where they cut it. In October. Don't tell me that's nothing.

after_burnt.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
after_burnt.text: Standing, and nothing walks out of the ricks. The undercroft's cold. -- I'll fill the stair in this winter. A harvest that's waited fifty years doesn't want carrying out. It wants letting go.

bye.speaker: Dunnock Southgate
bye.text: If you see straw walking, walk the other way.
